raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old male, diagnosed as HIV-positive, presented to our department with multiple painful, erythematous skin lesions over extremities, face and abdomen of 2 days duration along with the history of evening rise of temperature with chills, malaise, body pains, joint pains, and ankle edema. The patient had history of nasal stuffiness and epistaxis. He was not a known case of leprosy. He was on ART zidovudine, lamivudine, nevirapine (ZLN) for 4 weeks prior to the onset of skin lesions. Further, history of sexual exposure with multiple heterosexual partners was noted. No history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or tuberculosis.
On general examination, he was pale, thin built, ill nourished and febrile. On examination, there was no generalized lymphadenopathy. There was diffuse infiltration of ear lobe [Figure 1]. Multiple erythematous, tender papules, and nodules were present on the face [Figure 2] and also on trunk and extremities [Figure 3]. Sensations of pain and touch were reduced over both the feet. Ulnar, radial cutaneous, lateral popliteal, and posterior tibial nerves on both sides were thickened and tender. Hair, nails and mucous membranes were normal. Systemic Examination revealed no abnormalities.
Hematological Examination revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia (Hb: 10 g%), and neutrophilic leukocytosis (TLC: 12,800/mm3) differential count N75L20M3E2, and raised ESR (68 mm in-first hour). VDRL was non-reactive, and HBsAg was negative. The findings of complete urine examination were normal. Blood glucose levels, renal function and liver function tests were normal. Chest X-ray and ultrasonography of abdomen were normal. HIV-1 was reactive, the viral load was 1,07,400 copies/mL and CD4 count 94 cells/cu. mm before starting ART. At the time of diagnosis of IRIS, which is 1 month after starting of ART, CD4 count was 151 cells/cu. mm. Slit skin smear examination for M. leprae revealed bacteriological index of 4 along with a morphological index of 20%. Biopsy taken from the nodule on the left hand [Figure 3] demonstrated mild hyperkeratosis in epidermis, grenz zone. Dermis shows edema with collection of macrophages [Figure 4]. Vessels showed acute and chronic perivascular inflammatory infiltrate [Figure 5] consistent with ENL.
On the basis of the history, clinical examination, and investigative findings, a diagnosis of IRIS presenting as ENL in a patient of HIV with unmasking of lepromatous leprosy was made.
The patient was continued on ART and started on MBMDT (rifampicin:-600 mg, dapsone:- 100 mg, and clofazamine:-50 mg). He was given oral steroids which were gradually tapered over a period of 3 months. After 9 months of MBMDT and ART, no further episodes of ENL were reported and his CD4 count is 367. The patient is doing fine and attending to his duties.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old HIV-positive male presented 4 weeks after initiating antiretroviral therapy with a 2-day history of multiple painful erythematous skin lesions over his face, abdomen, and extremities, evening fever with chills, arthralgia, myalgia, and ankle edema.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having started antiretroviral therapy (zidovudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine) 4 weeks earlier, the patient acutely developed painful erythematous papules and nodules over his extremities, face, and abdomen for 2 days, accompanied by evening fevers with chills, malaise, generalized body aches, joint pains, ankle swelling, nasal stuffiness, and epistaxis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with HIV-1 infection (baseline CD4 94 cells/mm3, viral load 107,400 copies/mL) and treated with ZLN ART for 4 weeks; history of unprotected sex with multiple heterosexual partners; no prior history of known leprosy, diabetes, hypertension, or tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for evening fever, chills, malaise, myalgia, arthralgia, ankle edema, nasal stuffiness, epistaxis, and painful skin nodules.

objective.physical_examination: The patient was febrile, pale, thin, and undernourished without generalized lymphadenopathy, and systemic visceral exam was normal. Cutaneous examination revealed diffuse earlobe infiltration and multiple tender erythematous papules and nodules over the face, trunk, and extremities, with normal hair, nails, and oral mucosa. Neurological examination demonstrated reduced pain and light touch sensation over both feet and bilateral thickening and tenderness of the ulnar, radial cutaneous, lateral popliteal, and posterior tibial nerves.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematological workup revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 10 g/dL), neutrophilic leukocytosis (TLC 12,800/mm3; differential N75 L20 M3 E2), and elevated ESR (68 mm/1st hour). CD4 count at presentation (1 month post-ART) had risen to 151 cells/mm3 (from 94 cells/mm3 pre-ART). Blood glucose, liver and renal function tests, urinalysis, VDRL, HBsAg, chest X-ray, and abdominal ultrasound were normal or negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Slit-skin smear and a left hand nodule biopsy were performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Slit-skin smear demonstrated a Bacteriological Index (BI) of 4+ and Morphological Index (MI) of 20% for Mycobacterium leprae, and left hand nodule biopsy showed mild epidermal hyperkeratosis, a subepidermal Grenz zone, dermal edema with macrophage collections, and acute-on-chronic perivascular leukocytoclastic inflammatory infiltrates, confirming unmasking multibacillary lepromatous leprosy presenting with Type 2 reaction (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL) as an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Antiretroviral therapy was continued alongside standard WHO multibacillary multidrug therapy (rifampicin 600 mg, dapsone 100 mg, and clofazimine 50 mg) and a 3-month tapering course of oral corticosteroids; at 9-month follow-up, he remained reaction-free with a CD4 count of 367 cells/mm3.
